artworks.title: Staircase of a Palace
artworks.medium: Pen and brown ink over graphite on paper.
artworks.description: This sheet retains traces of an underdrawing that reveals the careful attention paid to an accurate projection of the perspective. Bibiena sets would not have included painted figures, so this drawing might record a live production (perhaps as a preparatory study for a commemorative engraving). Alternately, it could be an independent drawing exercise.

artworks.title: Partial View of a Circular Palace Hall with Radiating Rooms, a Design for the Stage
artworks.medium: Pen and brown ink and wash, over graphite, on paper.
artworks.description: This exuberantly ornate space was drawn in Antonio Bibiena's typically animated, calligraphic style. The drawing represents an early stage in the creative process: sketched first in graphite, it was then worked up in pen, ink, and wash. The brilliantly abstracted figures beneath the arches and along the balustrade are characteristic of Antonio's lively designs.

artworks.title: Capriccio of Rome with Triumphal Arch and Neptune Fountain

artworks.description: Giuseppe Bibiena indulged his penchant for combining reality and fantasy, and ancient and Baroque, in his drawings for Architetture, e prospettive (Architecture, and perspectives). Published in 1740, the volume of engravings was dedicated to Emperor Charles VI and included depictions of court performances, sacred theater, and funerary monuments honoring the members of the imperial family. artworks.description: In 1836 two minor Venetian islands, San Cristoforo and San Michele were joined to become a single island that served as a burial ground for Venice. The city's dead were brought to the island, now known as San Michele, by a distinctive, ornate gondola, a conveyance that poet Percy Bysshe Shelley had already likened to a funeral bark when exploring the city with Byron in 1818. artworks.title: Double Portrait of the West Sisters
artworks.medium: Black and red chalk on paper.
artworks.description: At the time Vogelstein executed this portrait of the sisters Mary Catherine and Elizabeth West, he was a professor at the Dresden Academy and an accomplished portraitist who specialized in incisive pencil studies. He had spent seven years in Rome with the Nazarenes, and his lucid, linear style reveals the influence of their portraits. This sheet is a rare portrayal by Vogelstein outside the Dresden Kupferstichkabinett, which holds the majority of his drawn oeuvre of over 700 portraits.

artworks.title: Figures in a River Landscape with Bridge
artworks.medium: Black chalk and ink, heightened with white, and with traces of red chalk, on paper.
artworks.description: Giuseppe Zais worked in the long Venetian tradition of landscape, incorporating motifs that can be traced back to the work of Titian and Domenico Campagnola in the sixteenth century, but which continued in the work of his contemporaries and associates Marco Ricci and Francesco Zuccarelli. These are all seen in this impressive, large drawing, with its prominent foreground tree, bridge and ruins in the middle distance, and mountain peaks and clouds beyond.

artworks.description: Exhibition label: Baselitz's first upside-down drawings include several landscapes, often executed on pages removed from old books or ledgers. In this work from 1970 (upon which the artist later erroneously wrote "69"), the sideways direction of the text contributes to the disorientating effect, rendering the image more abstract. As a teenager, Baselitz had considered studying forestry before enrolling in art school. Trees would remain a frequent subject in his work.

artworks.medium: Gouache and ink on paper.
artworks.description: Exhibition label: Baselitz often depicts fir trees - abundant both in German forests and traditional German Romantic landscapes - in order to highlight his art's northern roots. In the work of Caspar David Friedrich (1774-1840), for instance, evergreen trees are central to conveying a transcendental vision of nature. In 1985 a visitor to Baselitz's studio noted that a reproduction of a picture of pine trees by Friedrich was tacked to the wall.

artworks.description: Exhibition label: M. D. are the initials of Marcel Duchamp (1887-1968), whom Baselitz has described as "terrible" at painting but whose lasting influence on contemporary art intrigued him. Here Duchamp appears to be wearing a dress, in a possible reference to his female alter ego, Rrose Sélavy (a pun on "Eros, c'est la vie"). artworks.title: A Sheet of Studies with a Woman in Profile, and other Sketches
artworks.medium: Black chalk over red chalk.
artworks.description: A typical sheet of studies by the classicizing seventeenth-century Venetian artist Carpioni, this drawing probably relates to one of the Bacchanals for which Carpioni is best known today, canvases packed with groups of clothed and nude figures akin to those seen here. Its relationship to a specific work, however, remains to be discovered.

artworks.title: A Gallant Couple
artworks.medium: Pen and brown ink and wash, black-brown wash, incised with metal stylus on paper.
artworks.description: The German artist Johann Liss is best known for the dramatic baroque paintings that he produced during the final decade of his life, when he lived in Rome and Venice. Earlier in his career, however, he worked in Haarlem and Amsterdam. This drawing surely dates to this earlier period, for the figures are akin to those in the courtly scenes and merry company compositions that Liss produced at that time, under the influence of his Dutch and Flemish contemporaries.
